extracted.intended_audience: PRSA members and public relations professionals
extracted.subtask_description: The PRSA Code of Ethics: a code of professional values and provisions of conduct for PRSA members, describing core principles, intents, guidelines, and examples of improper conduct to guide ethical public relations practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRSA Member Statement of Professional Values
rubrics_metrics.description: This statement presents the core values of PRSA members and, more broadly, of the public relations profession. These values provide the foundation for the Code of Ethics and set the industry standard for the professional practice of public relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the values are fundamental beliefs guiding behaviors and decision-making; they are intended to be the foundation for the Code and a model for other professions, organizations, and professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: We serve the public interest by acting as responsible advocates for those we represent. We provide a voice in the marketplace of ideas, facts, and viewpoints to aid informed public debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practitioners should promote client/organizational interests responsibly while contributing to informed public debate; advocacy must be balanced with other professional values (e.g., honesty, public interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: We adhere to the highest standards of accuracy and truth in advancing the interests of those we represent and in communicating with the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members must ensure accuracy and truthfulness in all communications and disclosures; honesty underpins trust with publics and media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: We acquire and responsibly use specialized knowledge and experience. We advance the profession through continued professional development, research, and education. We build mutual understanding, credibility, and relationships among a wide array of institutions and audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members should pursue ongoing professional development, apply specialized knowledge responsibly, and contribute to the profession's advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence
rubrics_metrics.description: We provide objective counsel to those we represent. We are accountable for our actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members must offer objective, independent counsel and accept responsibility for their professional actions and recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: We are faithful to those we represent, while honoring our obligation to serve the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members must balance fidelity to clients/employers with duties to the public interest; loyalty does not supersede ethical obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: We deal fairly with clients, employers, competitors, peers, vendors, the media, and the general public. We respect all opinions and support the right of free expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members are expected to treat stakeholders fairly, respect differing opinions, and uphold free expression in professional activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free Flow of Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Core Principle: Protecting and advancing the free flow of accurate and truthful information is essential to serving the public interest and contributing to informed decision making in a democratic society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent: maintain integrity of relationships with media, government officials, and the public; aid informed decision-making. Guidelines: preserve the integrity of communication processes; be honest and accurate; promptly correct erroneous communications for which the practitioner is responsible; ensure gifts are nominal, legal, and infrequent so as not to prejudice information flow. Examples of improper conduct: giving expensive gifts to influence coverage; entertaining a government official beyond legal/reporting limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Core Principle: Promoting healthy and fair competition among professionals preserves an ethical climate while fostering a robust business environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent: promote respect and fair competition; serve public interest by providing wide practitioner choice. Guidelines: follow ethical hiring practices that respect free and open competition; avoid deliberately undermining competitors; preserve intellectual property rights. Examples of improper conduct: sharing helpful information with a competing firm bidding for the same business; spreading malicious/unfounded rumors about a competitor to recruit their people or clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Core Principle: Open communication fosters informed decision making in a democratic society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent: build trust by revealing all information needed for responsible decision making. Guidelines: be honest and accurate; correct erroneous communications promptly; investigate truthfulness/accuracy of information released on behalf of those represented; reveal sponsors for causes/interests represented; disclose financial interests (e.g., stock ownership); avoid deceptive practices. Examples of improper conduct: operating front groups or undisclosed grassroots campaigns; lying by omission about financial information; failing to correct inaccurate website/media kit information; employing people to pose as volunteers for hearings/campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguarding Confidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Core Principle: Client trust requires appropriate protection of confidential and private information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent: protect privacy rights of clients, organizations, and individuals by safeguarding confidential information. Guidelines: safeguard confidences and privacy rights of present, former, and prospective clients and employees; protect privileged, confidential, or insider information; immediately advise appropriate authority if confidential information is being divulged by a client employee. Examples of improper conduct: changing jobs and using confidential information to the detriment of a former employer; intentionally leaking proprietary information to harm another party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Core Principle: Avoiding real, potential or perceived conflicts of interest builds the trust of clients, employers, and the publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent: earn trust and mutual respect with clients/employers; build public trust by avoiding or ending situations that put personal/professional interests in conflict with society’s interests. Guidelines: act in the best interests of the client/employer (even subordinating personal interests); avoid actions/circumstances that may appear to compromise judgment; disclose promptly any existing or potential conflicts to affected clients/organizations; encourage clients/customers to determine if a conflict exists after notification. Examples of improper conduct: failing to disclose strong financial interest in a client's competitor; representing a competitor or conflicting interest without informing a prospective client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhancing the Profession
rubrics_metrics.description: Core Principle: Public relations professionals work constantly to strengthen the public’s trust in the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent: build respect and credibility for the profession; improve, adapt and expand professional practices. Guidelines: acknowledge obligation to protect and enhance the profession; keep informed and educated about practices; actively pursue personal professional development; decline representation that urges actions contrary to the Code; accurately define what public relations activities can accomplish; counsel subordinates in ethical decision making and require their adherence to the Code; report practices that fail to comply with the Code. Examples of improper conduct: publicly declaring a product safe without disclosing contrary evidence; assigning questionable client work to a non-member to avoid ethical obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and Membership Discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on enforcement has been eliminated, but the PRSA Board retains the right to bar from membership or expel any individual who has been or is sanctioned by a government agency or convicted in a court of law of an action that fails to comply with the Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While active enforcement emphasis is reduced, PRSA reserves disciplinary authority tied to government sanctions or criminal convictions related to Code noncompliance; ethical practice remains the primary obligation and the Code is considered a model for others.
